analysis.one_liner: Imposes a 90% income tax on bonuses paid by companies rescued with federal bailout money.
analysis.headline: The bill to tax 90% of bonuses paid by bailed-out banks was referred to the Ways and Means Committee in March 2009 and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After the 2008 financial crisis, the government rescued failing banks and insurers with taxpayer money under the Troubled Asset Relief Program (TARP). This bill would have added a 90% surtax on any bonus paid by one of those rescued companies, so that executives and employees keeping bailout-funded bonuses would send nearly all of it back to the Treasury. Regular wages, commissions, and benefits would not have been touched, and the tax would have stopped once a company fully repaid its bailout. The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal taxpayers, in the narrow sense that bailout money paid out as bonuses at rescued firms would have been partly recouped by the Treasury. The bill was aimed at executives and high earners at TARP-assisted companies, who would have borne the 90% surtax.

how_it_helps.text: It imposed a 90% surtax on bonuses paid by any company that received TARP financial assistance, so much of any bailout-funded bonus would go back to the Treasury instead of to executives.
The tax covered companies in the same corporate group, including foreign subsidiaries in the group, making it harder to avoid by paying bonuses through an affiliate.

It protected ordinary pay: regular hourly, daily, weekly, or monthly wages, commissions, benefits, and expense reimbursements were excluded from the tax, and the tax stopped applying once a company had fully repaid its TARP assistance.

analysis.who_pays: Executives and employees of companies that received TARP bailout assistance, who would have had 90% of any bonus taken by the tax, and the companies themselves, which would have faced pressure to repay the bailout quickly to shield future bonuses.

drawbacks.text: The tax applied retroactively to bonuses already paid after 2008, and punishing compensation after the fact raises fairness questions — the same concern that stalled a similar 90% AIG bonus tax in the Senate in 2009, where critics warned it could amount to punishing people for lawful income under rules adopted after the fact.

The bill taxed individual employees rather than the companies, so it targeted the people who received bonuses rather than the firms' bonus policies themselves; its main practical effect may have been to pressure TARP firms to repay the government quickly (after which the tax would no longer apply) rather than to change compensation practices permanently.
It was a one-time levy tied only to TARP assistance, so it would not have affected bonuses at other large financial firms that did not receive bailout funds.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit was straightforward: money the government put into rescued banks would partially come back through taxes on large bonuses, and executives would think twice about paying bonuses out of public funds. The costs are real, though: a 90% rate aimed at compensation already paid raises retroactive-fairness questions (the same objection that stalled the similar AIG bonus tax in the Senate), and a one-time levy on individuals does nothing to change how bailout recipients are regulated going forward. On balance it was a targeted, defensible response to a moment of public anger, but it was a narrow tax measure, not a fix for bailout oversight.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it sat there until that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mike Thompson introduced the bill on March 17, 2009, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action — the bill never moved after its referral.
The bill attracted only two cosponsors, both House Democrats, and no further support developed.
The 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, and the bill expired in committee without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Executives and employees of TARP bailout recipients kept their bonuses untaxed, and the bailed-out banks avoided the political and financial pressure a 90% bonus tax would have created. Taxpayers did not recover any of that money through this route.

for.name: Mike Thompson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to impose a 90% tax on bonuses paid by TARP-assisted businesses.

for.name: 2 of 253 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no other members signed on and no other action followed.

against.name: Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on March 17, 2009 and took no further action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Charlie Rangel
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: As chairman of the committee holding the bill, never scheduled it for consideration; the bill died in his committee.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Democratic sponsor and two Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support on record, and it died in a Democratic-controlled committee without ever reaching the floor.

industries.industry: Executives and employees of TARP bailout recipients
industries.note: Their bailout-year bonuses would have been taxed at 90%, returning most of the money to the Treasury. The tax applied until their firm fully repaid its government assistance.

The bill did not tax the firms directly, but it would have pressured them to restructure compensation and to repay TARP quickly so the tax would stop applying. The broader effect was to raise the political and financial price of paying large bonuses out of public rescue money.
Public money funneled into bonuses at rescued firms would have been partly recovered through the tax. The bill existed to protect taxpayers from funding bonus checks with bailout dollars.
